title: Urban Farming
description: Four recordings about growing food in cities: a radio report from a rooftop farm, a council meeting, a lecture on vertical farming and a radio phone-in.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A rooftop farm
parts.intro: You will hear a radio reporter, Sofia, interviewing Carlos, who runs a farm on a city roof.

script.speaker: Sofia
script.text: I'm standing on the roof of a former car park in the middle of the city, and instead of cars, I'm surrounded by tomatoes, lettuce and, believe it or not, a few beehives. With me is Carlos, who started this farm four years ago. Carlos, how did it begin?

script.speaker: Carlos
script.text: Honestly, it began as a hobby. I worked in an office on the ground floor of this building, and I used to stare at the empty roof during lunch breaks. One day I asked the owner if I could grow a few vegetables up here. He said yes, mostly because he thought I'd give up within a month.

script.speaker: Sofia
script.text: But you didn't give up.

script.speaker: Carlos
script.text: No, and now we employ twelve people and supply six local restaurants. We also sell boxes of vegetables to about two hundred households every week.

script.speaker: Sofia
script.text: What are the advantages of growing food in the city?

script.speaker: Carlos
script.text: Freshness, mainly. Our salad leaves are picked in the morning and eaten the same evening, just a few streets away. There's no long journey, so there's far less pollution from transport, and nothing spoils on a lorry.

script.speaker: Sofia
script.text: And the difficulties?

script.speaker: Carlos
script.text: Wind is the big one. It's much stronger up here than at ground level, so we've had to build special screens. And we rely entirely on rainwater, which we collect in tanks, because the building's water supply is expensive.

script.speaker: Sofia
script.text: Do people ever complain about the bees?

script.speaker: Carlos
script.text: Surprisingly rarely. Most visitors are simply fascinated. We run tours at weekends, and the honey is by far the most popular product.

parts.title: Part 2 · A meeting with a councillor
parts.intro: You will hear a resident, Mai, talking to a councillor, Mr Rashid, about a plan for a community garden.

script.speaker: Mr Rashid
script.text: Thank you for coming, Mai. I understand you'd like to turn the empty plot behind the library into a community garden.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: That's right. It's been unused for nearly ten years, and it's become a place where people dump rubbish. About forty neighbours have signed a petition supporting the idea.

script.speaker: Mr Rashid
script.text: Forty is encouraging. Now, I should be honest about the obstacles. First, the land belongs to the council, so you'd need a lease, and that takes about three months to arrange.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Three months is fine. We wouldn't plant until spring anyway.

script.speaker: Mr Rashid
script.text: Second, the soil. Land like this is often contaminated, so we'd have to test it. The test costs about three hundred pounds.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: We hadn't budgeted for that. Could the council cover it?

script.speaker: Mr Rashid
script.text: I can't promise, but I'll raise it at the next meeting. Realistically, I'd say it's likely, since you're offering to do the rest of the work.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: That's good news. And if the soil is poor, we could use raised beds, couldn't we?

script.speaker: Mr Rashid
script.text: Yes, that's a sensible backup plan. Third, who will look after the garden? Community projects often start with great enthusiasm, then fade after six months.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: I've thought about that. We'll create a rota, and the primary school next door has already offered to send a class every Friday.

script.speaker: Mr Rashid
script.text: Excellent. That's the kind of detail that persuades the committee. Send me a short written plan by the end of the month.

parts.title: Part 3 · A lecture on vertical farming
parts.intro: You will hear part of a lecture by Professor Hughes.

script.speaker: Professor Hughes
script.text: Good afternoon. Today I'd like to introduce vertical farming, which is perhaps the most dramatic form of urban agriculture. Instead of spreading crops across fields, vertical farms stack them in layers inside a building, sometimes twenty or thirty shelves high.

script.speaker: Professor Hughes
script.text: There are no windows and no soil. The plants grow in trays of water, enriched with nutrients, under coloured lights. Because everything is controlled, the farm doesn't depend on the weather. A crop that takes two months outdoors may be ready in four weeks.

script.speaker: Professor Hughes
script.text: The environmental advantages are significant. These farms use up to ninety per cent less water than traditional agriculture, because the water is recycled. They need no pesticides, since insects can't get in, and they can be built next to the customers, which cuts transport.

script.speaker: Professor Hughes
script.text: However, I want to be clear that the picture is not entirely rosy. Lighting uses a huge amount of electricity. If that electricity comes from coal, the carbon benefits largely disappear. Several well-known companies have already gone bankrupt, partly because their energy bills were higher than expected.

script.speaker: Professor Hughes
script.text: There's also a limit to what can be grown. At the moment, vertical farms are excellent for leafy greens and herbs, but they can't compete on staples such as wheat or rice, which need space and sunshine.

script.speaker: Professor Hughes
script.text: My own view, then, is that vertical farming is a useful addition, rather than a replacement for traditional farms. It's best seen as a way to produce fresh, perishable food close to where it is eaten.

parts.title: Part 4 · A radio phone-in
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter, Jenny, talking to a caller, Ahmed, about urban farming.

script.speaker: Jenny
script.text: Our topic today is whether urban farming could ever feed a whole city. We have Ahmed on the line. Ahmed, what do you think?

script.speaker: Ahmed
script.text: I'm sorry, Jenny, but I think it's a lovely idea that is being oversold. I live in a city of three million people. To feed all of them, you'd need farmland many times larger than the city itself. A few rooftops won't change that.

script.speaker: Jenny
script.text: That's a fair point. Do you see no value at all, then?

script.speaker: Ahmed
script.text: No, I wouldn't say that. For the community, it's wonderful. Children learn where food comes from, neighbours meet, and fresh vegetables become available in places where the nearest supermarket is miles away. I just don't think it solves the food problem.

script.speaker: Jenny
script.text: Some experts say cities could produce about a fifth of their vegetables locally.

script.speaker: Ahmed
script.text: A fifth is useful, I'll grant you, but vegetables are only a small part of our diet. People get most of their calories from grains and meat, which can't be grown on a balcony.

script.speaker: Jenny
script.text: So what would you prefer the council to spend money on?

script.speaker: Ahmed
script.text: Honestly, I'd rather see support for small farms outside the city, and better roads and trains to bring their produce in. Combine that with community gardens, and you get something realistic.

script.speaker: Jenny
script.text: Thank you, Ahmed. Interesting to hear a cautious voice. We'll take another call after the news.
